job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Hana Varga

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for sitting down with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I share a flat in Brenner with two friends, Lena who's a nurse and Mira who's in teacher training. My mornings are spent on applications, the afternoon at the library or the gym, and evenings cooking for everyone, because I'm the one who enjoys it. I finished a finance degree at Brenner University last summer with a pass and no internship. I wanted the graduate scheme at a big bank, but I failed their online test twice. My mum's a dentist and she's said I can lean on her if the rent gets tight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's what I'd expect: some boring tasks speed up, the rest stays the same. I'd tell people to be curious about it and not to swallow either the hype or the doom.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'm already worried, and that's before AI. Five months without a job offer, and a failed bank test, makes me wonder whether my degree is just a bit average. My flatmates are secure, which is lovely and a bit painful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply to more mid-sized companies and not only the big banks, about 10 a week. I'd practise the online tests properly, there are free ones. I'd ask Mum if her dentist friends know any accountants. And I'd use AI to polish my CV, which I do now and then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A mix. I'm not panicking, because I have savings and Mum. But I feel a low hum of failure. When someone asks, so, what are you doing now?, it stings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the bank test. How did it feel to fail it twice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it felt like the test measured how well I handle puzzles at speed, not how good I'd be with numbers. But I also knew I hadn't practised enough. Both can be true.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do differently if it's all just routine?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much, because in that world the same bank tests exist. I'd practise them like an exam, in the same time limits, with a friend marking me. I think I just under-prepared.

Be **curious** and swallow neither the hype nor the doom.
think: I'm already worried before AI, because **five months** without an offer and a failed bank test make my degree feel average.
My flatmates being secure is nice and painful.
do: Apply to **10 mid-sized companies** a week instead of only big banks.
Practise online **aptitude tests** with a friend marking me.
Ask Mum if her dentist friends know any **accountants**.
feel: A mix of **calm** and a low hum of failure when someone asks what I'm doing now.

fieldNote: The worry is the **job search itself**, not AI, and she names her own under-preparation.
Fair-minded: holds both the test's flaws and her own **weak prep**.
Flatmates' security highlights her sense of lagging behind.

steps.text: Send 10 applications a week to mid-sized firms
Practise timed online aptitude tests with a friend
Ask Mum's friends for accountant introductions

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going to change entry roles, and we'll see it in graduate schemes first. I'd say firms and universities both should be more honest about it. I'd also say not everyone can just go and learn to code.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the job I'm trying for might get smaller. Banks and accountancy firms say graduate numbers are under review. The routine bits like reconciliations and report drafts are what the software does well. I might be applying for a shrinking door.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the tools properly, probably a data analysis tool and a more advanced spreadsheet course. I'd apply to roles that mention data or analytics, which feel safer. I'd keep my flat share, because moving back home feels like retreat, and use Mum's help only if I need it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I'm managing it. I'd write lists and take a run. It's fine when I do something, and it's bad when I just scroll the news.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which jobs do you think survive best?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Roles where someone has to talk to people, explain, and take responsibility. Advisory work, client relations, anything where trust matters. I don't think all accounting disappears, but the first rungs get thinner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much of the CV polishing do you hand to AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only the first draft and the grammar. I always rewrite after. I don't trust it to say what I'd really say, and recruiters can spot generic CVs now.

Not everyone can just learn to code.

steps.text: Take a data analysis course this winter

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a huge risk, and we should push for proper safety nets like income support and retraining. I'd say it calmly, because panic won't help. I'd also say nobody knows exactly how it'll go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm scared. If all thinking jobs go, finance is first. I'd have to go for something practical, and I'm not sure what. Lena's nursing job feels safer, which I'd never have said a year ago.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop spending on anything extra, and I'd ask Mum for her honest view on what I should do. I'd look at healthcare administration or something hands-on that lasts until 2031. I'd spend six months on a practical qualification, and keep applying while I do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, tired and strangely quiet. It's like a storm warning where you can't get to shelter, you just have to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your flatmates that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them I'm scared and that I might need to rethink everything. Lena would say come and look at healthcare. Mira would say it's too early to decide. Probably both are a little right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is it better or worse to know a date?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Better, if the date is real. Worse if it's wrong, because then I changed my life for nothing. I'd rather know and prepare than not know and be caught out.

say: It's a huge risk, so we need **income support** and retraining, said calmly because panic won't help.
Nobody knows exactly how it'll go.
think: I'm scared, because if all thinking jobs go, **finance** is first.
Lena's nursing job feels safer, which I'd never have said a year ago.
do: Stop extra **spending** and ask Mum what she honestly thinks I should do.
Look at **healthcare administration** or hands-on work that lasts until 2031.
Do a six-month **practical qualification** while still applying.
feel: **Scared**, tired and strangely quiet, like a storm warning with no shelter.
S2.quote: Lena's nursing job feels safer, which I'd never have said a year ago.
fieldNote: Her **flatmate's nursing job** gives a real comparison for 'safe' work.
Stays calm in speech but admits fear, and the **say/think gap** is clear.
Mum's judgment is a trusted resource.

steps.text: Cut extra spending and track every expense
Ask Mum for her honest view on my options

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the kind of warning that lets us act if we start. Retraining, rules for firms, some kind of safety net. I'd say it's fair for both employers and universities to prepare people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm anxious, but I can see a way through. If I get a first job soon, I'd have three or four years of experience, and I could shift into advice or client work. If I don't, I'd go for the healthcare admin route.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply hard for the next six months, then take the first decent offer. I'd learn the AI tools properly on the job. I'd save about 40 percent of my pay. And I'd think about Mum's practice, which needs someone to manage billing and insurance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not great, not terrible. A bit like waiting for exam results. You can plan, but not control it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is different about five years for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say don't count on the graduate scheme. Apply widely, learn the tools, and have a second plan. And don't treat a rejection as a verdict. I did, for a while, and it wasted time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you tell younger finance students anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years feels like panic, five feels like planning. With five I can build on a job, not scramble for any job.

say: Five years is a warning that lets us **act** if we start now.
We need retraining, rules for firms and a **safety net**.
think: I'm anxious but see a way through: a first job gives me **three or four years** of experience.
If not, healthcare admin is my backup.
do: Apply hard for **six months**, then take the first decent offer.

feel: **Not great, not terrible**, like waiting for exam results.
S3.quote: Don't count on the graduate scheme. Apply widely, learn the tools, and have a second plan.
fieldNote: She turns her **rejection** into advice for others, which shows growth.

steps.text: Apply hard for six months then accept the first decent offer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is plenty, as long as people actually use it. I'd say we need to teach people tools and judgement together. And I'd be wary of anyone who says they know exactly how it'll turn out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be fine. At 33 I could have a decent career and have shifted into advisory or compliance. A decade makes a gradual change, not a cliff. My biggest risk is still the first job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get the first job, then do a professional qualification in finance, like a chartered finance course. I'd use AI tools in the work, and I'd save for a flat. I'd stay in touch with Lena and Mira, because we help each other.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. Like looking at a weather forecast ten days out. You check it, you pack an umbrella, but you don't cancel the trip.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, is any of this still urgent?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, yes. It's not urgent for 2036, but the next six months decide whether I start well. That part is urgent, and it has nothing to do with AGI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do differently now, if so?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do less panicking in the first months. I've learned I can plan once I stop treating each rejection like a verdict.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2031 one, strangely, because it's fast enough to scare me and slow enough that I'd have to live with the worry for years. What would help is clear honesty from firms about graduate numbers, free practice and training, and a small safety net while people retrain.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'm more worried about being average than about AI. A lot of my stress is the job hunt itself, and I think a lot of graduates feel the same but don't say so.

headlineQuote: I'm more worried about being average than about AI.
portrait: Hana is a **23-year-old** finance graduate sharing a flat in Brenner, rejected twice by a bank's online test.
She is **centre**, fair-minded, and blames both unfair tests and her own thin preparation.
She is a **steady** adapter who uses AI for CV drafts and learns more tools when things look proven.
Her flatmates' nursing and teaching jobs make her feel behind, and she tends to be **anxious** once entry roles shrink.
Mum's dental practice gives her a real fallback; she plans with decision points.
biggestWorry: She worries most about **AGI by 2031**, fast enough to scare her and slow enough to live with for years.
whatWouldHelp: Honest **graduate numbers** from firms, free practice and training, and a small safety net during retraining.
